To surfeit means to give, supply, or consume something in such excessive amounts that it stops being pleasurable and starts causing disgust, weariness, or a strong desire to have absolutely no more of it.

The word carries a specific, important quality: it is not just about having a lot of something. It is about crossing a line where the excess itself becomes the problem — where too much of even a good thing turns it sour, nauseating, or deeply unwelcome.

Think of eating your favourite food every single day, in enormous quantities, until the very smell of it repulses you. That journey from pleasure to revulsion through excess is the soul of this word.

The verb "surfeit" can be used in two main ways:

1. To surfeit someone (with something)
Here, one person or thing overwhelms another with something to the point of disgust or weariness. The subject is the one doing the overwhelming.

The royal court surfeited the guests with food, wine, and entertainment until nobody wanted any of it.

Years of empty praise had surfeited him, leaving him unable to trust even genuine compliments.

2. To surfeit oneself (on something)
Here, someone indulges themselves so excessively in something that they reach a point of revulsion or sickly fullness. The person is both the one doing the action and the one experiencing the consequence.

She had surfeited herself on celebrity gossip until it bored and disgusted her equally.

He surfeited himself on expensive wines over the years, and now even the finest bottle holds no excitement for him.

3. To be surfeited (passive form)
This describes the state of someone who has been brought to that point of excess and disgust.

After three hours of nonstop speeches, the audience was utterly surfeited and simply wanted to leave.

They were so surfeited with luxury that they found no joy in ordinary pleasures anymore.
The Critical Distinction: Why It's Stronger Than Similar Words

You might know words like satisfy, sate, or fill. Those words describe reaching a comfortable point of "enough." Surfeit goes further and beyond. Here's the spectrum:

  • Satisfy / sate → You've had enough. You feel content and complete. You don't need more, but you don't mind the sight of it.
  • Surfeit → You've had far, far too much. You are now weary of it, disgusted by it, or genuinely pained by it. The very thought of more feels unbearable.

This is why surfeit often carries a slight tone of consequence — the excess was not harmless. Something good was ruined by having too much of it.
It Applies to Far More Than Food

While the feeling is easy to understand through food, surfeit is used widely for anything that can be given or consumed in excess:

  • Praise and flattery: Constant flattery had surfeited her, and she found it hollow.
  • Entertainment or pleasure: A decade of parties and celebrations had surfeited him — he now craved quiet.
  • Information or stimulation: News channels had surfeited viewers with disaster coverage until they felt numb.
  • Sensory experience: The perfume shop surfeited her senses so completely that she had to step outside for air.
  • Love or attention (in excessive, smothering forms): He had been surfeited with affection as a child to the point where he resented closeness as an adult.

The key thread across all these uses: excess → weariness or disgust → no longer wanted.
The Tone and Register of This Word

Surfeit is a somewhat formal and literary word. You will encounter it more in books, essays, and elevated writing than in casual daily conversation. That said, using it in speech is entirely appropriate and marks you as precise with language.

It often appears in contexts that reflect on overindulgence as a human flaw or trap — the idea that chasing too much of something pleasurable can destroy the pleasure itself. Writers and thinkers use it to point out the irony that excess defeats its own purpose.

To surfeit is to overwhelm with such extreme excess — whether of food, pleasure, praise, stimulation, or anything desirable — that the recipient is left not just full or satisfied, but weary, disgusted, or sick of it entirely. It describes the moment when "too much" destroys the very enjoyment that the thing once offered. It can be done to someone else, to oneself, or felt passively as a state of being utterly glutted and repelled.
